comments.text:
[CORRECTIONS & UPDATES]

#####################

In the interest of fairness and full disclosure, I sometimes put a pinned comment here with any corrections and updates. Several people pointed out things about the video that are important to note:



1) 11:47 The Seven Cards, also known as the "Wason Selection Task". The point here is that we are asked 

"Which of these cards are worth turning over if you want to know whether the statement is false?"

So we must choose a card that DISCONFIRMS the statement. Human tendency to seek out confirming evidence is known as a "confirmation bias."

@user-kv2cl5dk9q  noted that:
"GPT-4 answers the 7 card problem (11:48) incorrectly. What’s interesting here is that GPT-4 falls for the same cognitive trap which catches out many human solvers, Wes."

So, the wording of the problem in the paper is more vague, asking which cards "Test" the statement vs which cards "determine whether the statement is *FALSE*"

Also, GPT-4 seems to be aware that this is the Wason selection problem.

I'll dig deeper and post more later below this.

comments.author: @benprytherch9202
comments.text:
I'm in general agreement with the "GPT-4 Can't Reason" paper, and I appreciate seeing this strong and reasonable critique.  Here's what I think the video misses.

The greatest strength of the paper, in my opinion, is its emphasis on how GPT-4 errs when it errs.  We know it's gonna err sometimes, and of course this isn't itself noteworthy; intelligent people err too.  It's the details of GPT-4's wrong answers that give off a "stochastic parrot" vibe.  Read through the back and forth dialog in the paper, especially what GPT-4 starts saying after giving its initial wrong answer.  It prints attempted solutions and then gives descriptions of its solutions that contradict what it just printed.  It guesses wildly, generating text that has the superficial structure of an explanation but means nothing.  The critque in "GPT-4 Can't Reason" is not just that it gets answers wrong.  The critique is that it devolves into printing incoherent nonsense when asked follow up questions.  This is what benchmarks cannot convey.  If GPT-4 is actually reasoning when it appears to be reasoning, why does it so quickly lose all these reasoning abilities in response to small changes in context and wording?  "Humans make mistakes too" won't cut it - read the paper and ask whether you think humans make mistakes *like those*.  Especially humans who just demonstrating impressive reasoning abilities to a nearly identical problem?  GPT-4 does this all the time.

In this video, GPT-4 is given big hints, advice, and clarifications that help it come to the correct solution.  In the furniture example, it's given a very strong hint that D needs to be by itself in the top row, and a pretty good hint that E needs to be in the right column, and then is given a "clarification" regarding the definition of adjacent that adds zero additional information regarding what "adjacent" means.  The first clarification of "adjacent" is a complete definition.  If that defintion doesn't make sense, the second clarification can't make sense either, since it depends upon the definition of "adjacent", and defining it both ways gives two perfectly logically identical statements.  So, why was this helpful?  I strongly suspect it's because additional clarifications always follow incorrect answers, so GPT-4 knows to try something else.  Also, note that the reasoning it prints in this video (go to 15:59) contains errors: it asserts there are two remaining cells in the middle row when there is only one, it asserts without justification that E must be in the last column (this ends up being true but showing that E cannot be in the 2nd column requires some extra steps), and it says that its two solutions are "the valid solutions", even though there are many more than these.

Ok, so why am I doing all this nit-picking?  After all, a human being might mostly solve such a problem properly, but make one or two minor errors when asked to write out step by step reasoning.  Doesn't GPT-4 deserve this same benefit of the doubt?

My answer is "no", on the grounds that we have an extremely plausible alternative explanation for how GPT-4 arrives at correct answers, one that doesn't apply to human beings.  It is that GPT-4 simply works the way it was designed to work.  It's a generative machine learning algorithm that was trained on most of what can be found on the internet plus lord knowns whatever else (OpenAI won't say).  These algorithms use patterns in the text it's seen (often very complex patterns!) to optimize a phenomenally large network for the purpose of predicting the next token.  There's more to it, but that's the gist.  So, we just saw GPT-4 get something almost right (but with some non-trivial errors mixed in), after being given the kinds of hints that a pattern seeking algorithm can readily take advantage of, and we have two explanations: 

1) GPT-4 is has somehow acquired an unexpected ability, akin to a human ability, and we don't really understand why on account of our incomplete understanding of the human mind and the challenge of interpreting specific output from a massive artificial deep learning network.
2) GPT-4 is operating as designed.

Now, I can't prove that 1) isn't happening.  Maybe somewhere in all the mystery lies the as-yet-unknown mechanism by which predictive algorithms develop broader inferential powers of the kind we recognize in ourself.  But maybe not.  My argument is basically Occam's Razor, which isn't deductive.  But it's compelling.

And this is why the long chat logs in "GPT-4 Can't Reason" are so important.  They are packed with examples that look far more like 2) than 1).  LLMs routinely swing back and forth between being unable to grasp extremely simple concepts and being able to give detailed and correct explanations of very difficult concepts.  This would be pretty weird if it was doing something anywhere near the ballpark of what we recognize as "reasoning".  It's not the least bit surprising if it's mindlessly generating plausible looking text using statistics.

comments.text: Okay Taco Bell employee number 3391112, how then do you expect us to reconcile this demonstration of yours with the utterly illogical and fantastical way LLMs get things wrong? As incredulous as you, or hell even Gary are being, I don't think you'd disagree with me when I say that LLMs don't think the way people do. If a student came up to you with a problem and was wrong in the same way that an LLM gets problems wrong, you would suspect brain damage. The adjacency problem is a good example. If a human didn't understand that A next to B is the same as B next to A, then you'd rightfully be concerned. The problem was not ambiguity, it was the lack of a model of the world. Just because you don't know where in the training data a similar task was found, doesn't mean that it isn't just copying from it. This is what happens when you take a chunk of data far too large for humans to analyze quickly, and then you start attributing magical traits to it every time you don't understand how it solved a problem. The default assumption for LLMs is that they don't know. Everything they say is just a prediction of the next token,so they are literally just guessing every time. If you whip something into shape with enough right and wrong answers, eventually it's going to appear to know. The reality is that you just molded it into what you want to see. Just think about it this way. Logically speaking what's more difficult, creating an intelligent problem solving machine with true reasoning capabilities, or creating a machine that appears to be smart most of the time? I mean is it easier to photoshop a picture of you, or is it easier to actually put the time in at the gym to build muscles? I think the answer is obvious. You're basically being catfished by a machine and you're mad about it.
